refuse the embedding?

"""Distributed Training From Scratch — stage 5: Tensor parallel

Stage 1 froze the shapes and the counters; stages 2 to 4 shard the **state** (the
gradients, the optimizer, the parameters) over a group. This stage shards the
**computation**: one projection's weight and its activation are cut across the
group, every rank multiplies its own block, and the two halves of the block
combine what they must with one all-reduce each and nothing else.

The block is one MLP projection pair: a **column-parallel** half followed by a
**row-parallel** half. In the column half each rank owns a contiguous block of
the projection's *output neurons*, multiplies the full input by its own rows of
the weight, and holds a *disjoint* slice of the result — no rank needs anything
from another, so this half costs no fabric at all. In the row half each rank
owns a matching block of the second projection's *input features*: every rank
multiplies its shard of the intermediate by its own block, and what it holds is
a **partial** sum, not yet the projection's output. Only the all-reduce over the
group turns those partials into the answer.

`reference_layer` is the arithmetic all of this must reproduce, **exactly**:
`y[i][j] = b[j] + sum_k x[i][k] * w[j][k]`, one row of `w` per output neuron.
`column_parallel` and `row_parallel` are the two halves on one rank's own
blocks; `f` and `g` are those two halves under the names the fixture composes.
A check that slices a weight into blocks, applies the halves across a group and
sums what the collectives carry must land on `reference_layer`'s own `int`s —
not near them — and must land there for every split of the group. Every number
here is an `int`, on the fixture matrices and in the plan.

`tensor_parallel` turns the block into the `StepPlan` stage 1 froze: the
collectives the block issues, in the order it issues them. A block issues two —
the forward's all-reduce at the row-parallel boundary, where the partials
become the projection's output, and the backward's all-reduce where the
gradient enters the column-parallel half — and each moves the block's own
activation, `batch * seq * hidden` elements per rank.

DESIGN DECISION — why do the two halves split the weight differently?
    They must, because the two halves leave *different things* on a rank. The
    column half's ranks produce disjoint slices of the projection's output, so
    splitting the weight one row per output neuron leaves each rank holding a
    complete answer for its own columns and the group needs no fabric at all.
    The row half's ranks each contract a *different* block of the input
    features, so every rank's result is a partial sum over the whole output and
    the all-reduce is what makes it an answer. The rejected alternative — split
    both halves the same way — either ends with an all-reduce that combines
    nothing (a block that pays the fabric for arithmetic it did not do) or ends
    with a partial that nothing combines (a block that is simply wrong while
    looking cheaper). Which half owns the bias is the same question: the half
    whose output is complete.

DESIGN DECISION — why two all-reduces per block, and what does one get wrong?
    The forward all-reduce is the row half's combine; the backward all-reduce
    is the gradient of the column half's input, which is a row-parallel
    traversal of the same shape and arrives as partials too. A block with a
    single all-reduce leaves one of the two uncombined: the forward keeps the
    row half's partials and the model's output is wrong by everything the other
    ranks contributed, or the backward keeps the column half's gradient
    partials and every rank descends along a fraction of the true gradient. Both
    failures are silent — the numbers stay the right shape and the right
    magnitude — which is why the count is asserted, not the flops.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the all-reduce sized by the block's activation?
    The tensor that crosses the fabric is the one the row half is summing: the
    projection's output, `batch * seq * hidden` elements per rank — one entry
    per token per output feature the model has at that point, `hidden`. Sizing
    it by the FFN's intermediate (`ffn_hidden`) charges the wider tensor the
    column half keeps sharded and never moves; sizing it for the whole layer, or
    by the parameter count, charges the model's size for one block's boundary.
    Both stay plausible and both are wrong by a factor, which is the arithmetic
    a real tensor-parallel estimate gets wrong first.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the algorithm chosen by price rather than fixed?
    A ring is the safe answer and the expensive one on this course's fixtures:
    on `switch(8, width=4)` the tree's fifty ticks beat the ring's hundred and
    eight for the same block, while the recursive doubling that ties the tree on
    `full(4)` cannot run across the spine at all (its XOR partners are three hops
    apart). That is I9's own rule and its own candidates: build every all-reduce
    `plans.py` can build, price each with `stage_01.plan_ticks` on the group's
    own fabric, drop a candidate whose preconditions fail instead of raising,
    keep the cheapest and break a tie by the candidate order. A fixed algorithm
    is a size table by another name, right on the fabric it was measured on.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a group of one an empty plan, not a one-rank
all-reduce?
    `plans.py`'s rule: a collective over one rank has nothing to combine, so its
    plan is empty and costs nothing. A `tp` axis of one that still emitted its
    two collectives would charge a step for traffic between a rank and itself —
    the "axis of one still emitting that axis's collectives" mistake stage 10
    names — so the block's plan has no collectives, no compute and no ledger,
    and a group of one is what makes the axis vanish rather than shrink.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the block's plan carry no compute?
    The compute a step spends belongs to the step and to its device, and
    `ComputeModel.compute_ticks` is where this course turns flops into ticks; a
    block's `shape` carries no device to do that with. What the block's plan
    states is the **traffic it adds** — its two all-reduces — so that a caller
    that owns a `ComputeModel` can price the whole step with stage 1's
    `step_ticks` (the maximum of the two). Inventing a compute here would either
    double-count the step's own or hide the traffic behind it.

TODO: implement `column_parallel`, `row_parallel`, `f`, `g` and `tensor_parallel`.
"""

import fabric
import model
import plans
import stage_01


def column_parallel(x, w):
    """The block's first half: one rank's slice of the projection's output.

    `x` is the full, replicated input activation, one row per token
    (`rows x inner`). `w` is the rank's block of the projection's weight, laid
    out the way `reference_layer` lays a weight out — one row per output neuron
    the rank owns, `out_local x inner`. The answer is `rows x out_local` with
    `y[i][j] = sum_k x[i][k] * w[j][k]`: the rank's own columns of the
    projection's output. The ranks' answers are disjoint and already in rank
    order, so nothing about this half crosses the fabric.

    A matrix that is not a non-empty tuple of equal-length `int` rows, and a
    weight whose inner dimension does not match the input's, are refused with
    `model.ModelError` naming the offender.
    """

    raise NotImplementedError("stage 5: implement column_parallel()")


def row_parallel(partial, w):
    """The block's second half: one rank's **partial** output.

    `partial` is the rank's shard of the intermediate activation, `rows x
    inner_local`, and `w` is the rank's block of the second projection's weight
    stored **one row per input feature the rank owns**, `inner_local x out`,
    because that is the block of the weight this rank holds. The answer is
    `rows x out` with `y[i][j] = sum_k partial[i][k] * w[k][j]`: a partial sum
    over the whole output, which the group's all-reduce turns into the
    projection's output.

    A matrix that is not a non-empty tuple of equal-length `int` rows, and a
    weight whose row count does not match the shard's column count, are refused
    with `model.ModelError` naming the offender.
    """

    raise NotImplementedError("stage 5: implement row_parallel()")


def f(x, w):
    """The block's first half under the name the fixture composes:
    `column_parallel(x, w)`, the column-parallel projection."""

    raise NotImplementedError("stage 5: implement f()")


def g(x, w):
    """The block's second half under the name the fixture composes:
    `row_parallel(x, w)`, the row-parallel projection whose answer is a partial
    until the forward all-reduce combines it."""

    raise NotImplementedError("stage 5: implement g()")


def tensor_parallel(shape, world, *, group, batch=1, seq=1):
    """One MLP block's `StepPlan`: the collectives the block issues, in order.

    `group` is the ranks the block is split over, in any order (the plan comes
    back in the world's rank order); `batch` and `seq` are the tokens the step
    runs, because the tensor at the row-parallel boundary is
    `batch * seq * hidden` elements per rank. The block issues two collectives —
    the forward's all-reduce of the row half's partials (`"activations"`) and
    the backward's all-reduce of the column half's gradient partials
    (`"grads"`) — chosen over `plans.py`'s legal all-reduce candidates by
    `stage_01.plan_ticks` on the group's own fabric. A layer repeats the pair
    once per projection (attention's query-key-value and output projections, the
    MLP's up and down projections); this plan is one block's.

    A `shape` that is not a `ModelShape`, a `batch` or `seq` that is not a
    positive count, and a group with a rank the world does not have, a rank
    named twice or no ranks at all are refused, naming the offender — the last
    three with the fabric's own `fabric.FabricError`. A group of one rank issues
    no collective: the block's plan is empty and costs nothing.
    """

    raise NotImplementedError("stage 5: implement tensor_parallel()")
files.stage_06.py:
"""Distributed Training From Scratch — stage 6: Pipeline parallel

A pipeline splits a model by layers: stage `s` owns a slice of the layers, and
the micro-batches flow through the stages. Nothing here talks to the fabric —
what this stage writes is a **schedule as data**: for every step and every
stage, which micro-batch is being forwarded and which is being back-propagated.
Everything the rest of the course says about a pipeline (its bubble, its memory,
its exit steps) is read off that data, never off a formula.

The data is a tuple of `Slot(step, stage, micro_batch, phase)`, where `phase` is
`"f"` for a forward and `"b"` for a backward, and it is **canonical**: sorted by
`(step, stage, phase, micro_batch)`, so two schedules that say the same thing
are equal.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a step numbered from one, and why does the forward of
micro-batch mu at stage s always sit at step `mu + s + 1`?
    Because the first stage has nothing to wait for and no stage can start a
    micro-batch before the stage above it has finished with it: micro-batch 0
    enters stage 0 at step 1, and after `p - 1` steps it reaches the last stage.
    Numbering from one makes "the last micro-batch leaves the last stage at
    `m + p - 1`" a sentence instead of an off-by-one argument, and pinning the
    forward stream is what makes the two schedules differ *only* in their
    backwards — which is exactly what they differ in.

DESIGN DECISION — why does a stage run at most one forward and one backward in
a step, and never two of either?
    One stage is one device with one set of weights: it can run one task at a
    time, and the name of the second schedule says what it does with that
    budget — one forward, one backward, of different micro-batches, in the same
    step. Two forwards in a step would need the stage to double its compute,
    and two backwards would need two sets of gradients to be applied at once;
    both are different machines, not different schedules.

DESIGN DECISION — why must a backward not share a step with the forward of its
own micro-batch?
    The backward needs that forward's activations. Putting them in the same step
    is asking a device to consume an activation in the step that produces it —
    a schedule that only works if every layer is instantaneous. This is the
    constraint the checks probe first, because it is the one a hand-written
    schedule violates most often.

DESIGN DECISION — why does GPipe's bubble survive its own backward pass, and why
is 1F1B's half of it?
    GPipe does every forward and then every backward, so no stage has a backward
    to run while the pipeline is still filling (and none has a forward to run
    once it is draining): its stages idle through a whole fill and a whole
    drain, `2p - 2` idle pairs each. 1F1B streams the backwards against the
    forwards, so a stage that has finished its part of a micro-batch's backward
    can take the next micro-batch's forward in the very next step; the same fill
    and drain are paid once and half of the pairs are saved. The formula is not
    the point — the replay is: for `(p, m) = (4, 8)` GPipe idles 24 pairs of the
    88 its makespan spends and 1F1B 12 of 60.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the bubble counted by replaying the slots, and why is
its fraction an exact pair?
    Because a formula is a claim and the slot list is the thing: replaying gives
    the makespan, the pairs that carry a task and the pairs that do not, and it
    is the only version of the number that survives a schedule someone wrote by
    hand. The fraction is `idle pairs / (stages x makespan)`, an exact rational —
    `3/11` for GPipe at `(4, 8)`, not `0.2727...` — because a course whose whole
    subject is counting does not round.

TODO: implement `gpipe`, `one_f_one_b`, `bubble`, `bubble_fraction` and `replay`.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass
from math import gcd

import model

#: The phases a slot can carry: a forward or a backward of one micro-batch.
PHASES = ("f", "b")


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Slot:
    """One task of one stage: the forward or the backward of one micro-batch,
    at one step. A stage can carry one `"f"` and one `"b"` in the same step."""

    step: int
    stage: int
    micro_batch: int
    phase: str


def gpipe(p, m):
    """`p` stages, `m` micro-batches: every forward, then every backward in
    reverse order. A tuple of `Slot`s, canonical.

    Refuses (`model.ModelError`, naming the offender) a count that is not a
    positive int. The backward of micro-batch `mu` at stage `s` sits at step
    `m + p + (m - 1 - mu) + (p - 1 - s)`, and the schedule must satisfy every
    dependency the module docstring lists.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 6: implement gpipe()")


def one_f_one_b(p, m):
    """`p` stages, `m` micro-batches, warm-up then a forward and a backward per
    stage per step then the cool-down: the backward stream runs against the
    forward stream, the last stage back-propagating first. A canonical tuple of
    `Slot`s, with the same refusals as `gpipe`.

    The backward of micro-batch `mu` at stage `s` sits at step
    `2p - s + mu`, which is what makes a stage's forwards and backwards share
    steps without ever sharing a micro-batch.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 6: implement one_f_one_b()")


def bubble(schedule, p):
    """The idle `(stage, step)` pairs inside the schedule's makespan: pairs that
    carry no task at all. A pair with one task is busy; a pair with two is still
    one pair.

    Refuses (`model.ModelError`, naming the offender) a schedule that is not a
    canonical tuple of `Slot`s over `p` stages, one that misses an
    `(micro_batch, stage, phase)`, one whose backward comes at or before its own
    forward, one whose forward does not follow the previous stage's, one whose
    backward does not follow the next stage's, and one that puts two tasks of
    the same phase in one step of one stage.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 6: implement bubble()")


def bubble_fraction(p, m, *, schedule):
    """The bubble over the `(stage, step)` pairs the makespan spends, as an
    exact pair `(idle, stages x makespan)` reduced to lowest terms with a
    positive denominator. No floats: `3/11`, never `0.2727...`.

    Refuses the same schedules `bubble` refuses, and a `p` or `m` that is not a
    positive int.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 6: implement bubble_fraction()")


def replay(schedule, p, m):
    """Each micro-batch's exit step — the step it leaves the pipeline, that is
    the largest step any of its slots is at — as a tuple of `m` ints, in
    micro-batch order. With `gpipe` the exits descend; with `one_f_one_b` they
    ascend.

    Refuses the same schedules `bubble` refuses.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 6: implement replay()")

"""Distributed Training From Scratch — stage 7: Pipeline schedules

Stage 6 wrote the two schedules as data; this stage adds the two things that
make a schedule a *scheduling* decision: **virtual stages** — a rank that owns
`v` chunks of the model instead of one — and **the memory the schedule holds
while it runs**. Nothing here talks to the fabric either: a schedule is still a
tuple of slots, read off the data and never off a formula.

Where stage 6's `Slot` carried `(step, stage, micro_batch, phase)`, this stage's
carries one more field, `chunk`: which of a rank's `v` chunks a task runs on. A
**unit** is one micro-batch's chunk — micro-batch `mu` and chunk `c` make the
unit `w = mu * v + c`, and there are `m * v` of them, with the `v` chunks of one
micro-batch consecutive in the unit order. The schedule is **stage 6's GPipe
over those `m * v` units**: unit `w` runs its forward at stage `s` at step
`w + s + 1`, and its backward there at step `2 * M + 2 * p - 2 - w - s` with
`M = m * v`. That one sentence is the whole of the interleaving, and it is why
`v = 1` must reproduce stage 6's `gpipe` exactly.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a chunk a virtual stage a rank owns, and not a second
micro-batch?
    Because the model is one model: splitting a micro-batch into `v` chunks is
    splitting its *layers*, not its tokens. The chunks of a micro-batch run on
    `v` different virtual stages, all of them owned by the ranks in the same
    order a single-chunk model would use, so a rank with `v` chunks can work on
    chunk `c` of a micro-batch and chunk `c + 1` of another in nearby steps.
    Reading `chunk` as a second micro-batch index would double the tokens and
    change the arithmetic, which is the one thing no plan here may do.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the schedule GPipe over the units, and what does the
bubble become?
    Because the interleaving does not change what work there is, only when the
    ranks do it: the `m * v` units are `m * v` micro-batches as far as the
    pipeline is concerned. GPipe's makespan for `N` micro-batches and `p` stages
    is `2N + 2p - 2`, so for `N = m * v` the idle `(stage, step)` pairs are
    `2p(p - 1)` and the fraction is `(p - 1) / (m * v + p - 1)` — for
    `(p, m, v) = (4, 8, 2)` the same `24` pairs stage 6 idles but over `152`
    instead of `88`, so `3/19` against `3/11`. The formula is not the point:
    the slots are, and replaying them is how the bubble is checked.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the bubble `(stage, step)` pairs and never a formula?
    Because a formula is a claim and the slot list is the thing. The check
    replays the tuple: the makespan is its largest step, a pair that carries one
    task is busy, a pair that carries two is still one pair, and the bubble is
    what is left over. That is the only version of the number that survives a
    schedule someone wrote by hand, and it is why this stage can assert
    `3/19` for `(4, 8, 2)` without an algebra of its own: the pair is exactly
    stage 6's GPipe bubble over `m * v = 16` micro-batches, recomputed there.

DESIGN DECISION — why does an activation live from its forward to its backward,
and why is the peak the union of the intervals?
    Because a pipeline trades memory for time in exactly that currency: the
    forward saves the activation its backward will consume, and the activation
    is dead the moment the backward has it. Its lifetime is therefore a range of
    steps — `(birth, death)`, born at the forward and dead at the backward — and
    the number of activations a rank holds at the peak is the number of those
    ranges that cover one step, which is a **union**: taking the longest single
    lifetime, or the bytes of one activation, undercounts a pipeline by the
    depth it is filled to, and that undercount is the whole mistake this stage
    exists to make visible.

DESIGN DECISION — why does `lifetime` refuse a schedule whose units do not
divide evenly over its chunks?
    Because `v` virtual stages per rank is a promise that each chunk carries the
    same number of units: a rank that owns `v` chunks has to be able to keep
    them fed, and a schedule that hands one chunk more work than another is not
    an interleaving, it is a schedule with an idle buffer and a live one. The
    count per chunk is read off the slots themselves, and the refusal names the
    counts it found.

TODO: implement `interleaved`, `lifetime` and `in_flight`.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass

import model

#: The phases a slot can carry: a forward or a backward of one micro-batch's
#: chunk.
PHASES = ("f", "b")


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Slot:
    """One task of one stage: the forward or the backward of one micro-batch's
    chunk, at one step. A stage can carry one `"f"` and one `"b"` in the same
    step; `chunk` is which of the rank's `v` virtual stages the task runs on."""

    step: int
    stage: int
    micro_batch: int
    phase: str
    chunk: int


def interleaved(p, m, v):
    """`p` stages, `m` micro-batches, `v` virtual stages per rank: the schedule
    as data, a canonical tuple of `Slot`s carrying the `chunk`.

    Stage 6's GPipe over the `m * v` units, unit `w = micro_batch * v + chunk`:
    the forward at stage `s` at step `w + s + 1`, the backward there at step
    `2 * (m * v) + 2 * p - 2 - w - s`. With `v = 1` it must reproduce stage 6's
    `gpipe(p, m)` exactly. Refuses `model.ModelError`, naming the offender, a
    `p`, `m` or `v` that is not a positive int.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 7: implement interleaved()")


def lifetime(schedule):
    """Each activation's `(birth, death)` step range, in `(micro_batch, chunk,
    stage)` order: born at the step its stage forwards it, dead at the step the
    same unit's backward at that stage consumes it.

    Refuses `model.ModelError`, naming the offender, a schedule that is not a
    canonical tuple of `Slot`s over its own `(p, m, v)`, one that misses a
    `(micro_batch, chunk, stage, phase)`, one whose backward is not after its
    own forward, one whose chunk order or stage order breaks the dependency, one
    that puts two tasks of the same phase in one step of one stage, and one
    whose units do not divide evenly over its chunks.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 7: implement lifetime()")


def in_flight(schedule, shape, *, batch, seq):
    """The bytes of the peak activations alive: the largest number of lifetimes
    covering one step — the union of the live intervals, never the longest one —
    times `shape.activation_bytes(batch, seq)`.

    Refuses `model.ModelError`, naming the offender, the schedules `lifetime`
    refuses, a `shape` that is not a `model.ModelShape`, and a `batch` or `seq`
    that is not a positive int.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 7: implement in_flight()")
files.stage_08.py:
"""Distributed Training From Scratch — stage 8: Expert parallel

An expert layer replaces one feed-forward network with a bank of them, and a
router sends every token to `top_k` of them. The tokens do not live where their
experts do, so the layer pays for **two** all-to-alls: the *dispatch*, which
carries each token to the expert that will process it, and the *combine*, which
carries the expert's output back to the rank that owns the token. This stage
writes the routing as data (`routing`), the two statistics the routing needs
(`dropped` and `balance_loss`), and the layer's `StepPlan`
(`expert_parallel`) — the two ragged exchanges, their lengths taken from the
routing, and the ledger of one expert per rank.

The routing is a **square table of placements**: `routing[source][expert]` is
the number of tokens the block on source rank `source` sends to expert
`expert`, so the table is exactly the `splits` table `plans.alltoall_from_splits`
takes, the row sums are what each rank dispatches and the column sums are the
experts' loads. Rows are the group's ranks in rank order and there is one
expert per rank, so the group is the world and its size is the expert count.
Every token of the block takes the `top_k` experts `(q + k) % experts`, which
are distinct because `top_k <= experts`; `hot=e` moves every token's last
choice to expert `e`, which leaves the row sums — the token count — untouched
and makes one column enormous. A capacity cap then limits how many placements
one (source, expert) cell keeps, and the combine carries back only what was
kept, so the combine is exactly `dropped` placements smaller than the dispatch.

Nothing here is measured: every number is an `int` (a fraction of a token is
not a thing this course can represent), the routing is a function of the shape,
the batch and the sequence alone, and two calls return equal values.

DESIGN DECISION — why two exchanges, and not one?
    A token is processed by an expert that lives on another rank, and its
    result must come home: the dispatch carries the token out, the combine
    carries the answer back, and they move the same kind of data in opposite
    directions. One all-to-all can only do the first half, so a plan with one
    exchange has silently dropped the experts' outputs — the token is processed
    and never returned. The two are separate collectives with separate lengths,
    because they do not move the same number of elements: the combine carries
    only the placements the capacity cap kept.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the exchange priced by the busiest rank, and not by
the mean?
    The whole layer waits for the rank that has the most to hand over. With
    `hot` the balanced row sums are unchanged — every rank still dispatches
    `tokens * top_k` placements in total — but one *expert*'s column is
    enormous, and on a rank whose own expert is hot the tokens it keeps cancel
    the ones it must send: one rank dispatches nothing at all while another
    dispatches its whole block. The mean of the sending ranks is then exactly
    the balanced figure, so a plan that charges the mean cannot tell a hot
    routing from a balanced one, and prices a stall the fabric never runs. The
    per-rank figure is therefore the maximum over the ranks of what one rank
    sends or takes in — the diagonal excluded, because the piece a token's own
    expert keeps on the token's own rank never crosses the fabric.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the combine carry fewer elements than the dispatch?
    The capacity cap exists because an expert's buffer is finite: a cell may
    keep `capacity_factor` times the routing's mean cell, and the placements
    beyond it are dropped. The dispatch still carries every placement — the
    token crossed the fabric whether or not the expert accepted it — but the
    combine carries only what the experts kept, so the difference between the
    two exchanges is exactly `dropped`, in placements. A cap that drops tokens
    and does not count them leaves the two exchanges equal, and the plan then
    claims a fabric that returned tokens no expert ever processed.

DESIGN DECISION — why is `balance_loss` an integer, and which integer?
    A softmax load-balancing loss is a float, and this course has no floats: a
    statistic that cannot be written as a whole count cannot be compared. The
    statistic used here is `experts * sum(load ** 2) - sum(load) ** 2` — the sum
    of the squared deviations of the expert loads from their mean, scaled by the
    expert count so that no fraction ever appears. It is exactly zero when every
    expert carries the same load and grows as one expert takes more, which is
    all a router needs to know; a mean-minus-max difference or a sum of absolute
    deviations would be a different (and coarser) number, and `dropped` alone
    would hide an imbalance that has not yet overflowed the cap.

DESIGN DECISION — why is `hot` a keyword of the plan too?
    The plan is what must expose the cost of a routing, and the fixture that
    shows the cost is an unbalanced one: the same token count, a different

"""Distributed Training From Scratch — stage 9: Sequence / context parallel

When a sequence is too long for one device, context parallel splits it across a
group: rank `b` owns positions `b * seq / split .. (b + 1) * seq / split - 1`,
carries the query, key and value of those positions, and attends its queries
against *every* key in the sequence. A rank cannot hold every key, so the key
and value blocks — the KV blocks — travel the group's **ring**, one hop at a
time, and each rank folds the block it receives into an accumulator. `seq/split`
grows with the sequence, so the attention a rank computes grows with it, but the
KV a rank must keep at once is one block, not the whole sequence.

This stage is the two halves of that idea. `online_attention(blocks)` is the
accumulation: given the blocks a rank has seen, in the order it saw them, return
the exact `(numerator, denominator)` pair `model.reference_attention` returns for
the whole sequence — **for every split**, one block or four, equal blocks or
unequal. `context_parallel(shape, world, *, batch, seq, split)` is the price:
the KV blocks rotating the ring, wrapped as a `StepPlan` (stage 1) whose
collective is the `plans.py` all-gather that walks them hop by hop.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the accumulator an exact pair of integers, and why does
the reference reduce it to lowest terms?
    A normalized softmax would be a float, and a float is not the same number on
    two machines; the whole course is exact integers for exactly this reason.
    The pair `(sum of 2**s * v, sum of 2**s)` is the *unnormalized* attention,
    and because a common factor cancels in the ratio, its lowest-terms form is
    independent of how the sum was cut up. `reference_attention` reduces by
    `gcd`, so one block, two blocks or four blocks of the same sequence return
    the *identical* pair, and a student can compare ints with `==`.

DESIGN DECISION — why must the running pivot only *drop*, and why do both parts
shift with it?
    A weight is `2 ** (score - pivot)`, held as an integer, so the pivot must be
    no larger than every score seen or the weight is a fraction — which an `int`
    accumulator cannot hold. The pivot therefore starts at the first block's
    lowest score and only ever falls, and when a later block is lower, `num` and
    `den` are both shifted left by the difference of the pivots before the block
    is folded in (`num <<= old - new`, `den <<= old - new`). Shifting only the
    numerator multiplies the ratio by a power of two and silently changes the
    answer, which is the mistake this stage exists to catch. This is the
    flash-attention max-rescale written so the weights stay whole numbers.

DESIGN DECISION — why does a rank keep its query block and stream the KV blocks,
rather than recompute each block on its own?
    Context parallel fixes each rank's queries and moves the keys to them, so the
    accumulator must survive between blocks: block `b`'s contribution is added to
    what blocks `0 .. b-1` left behind, and the running pivot makes the addition
    exact. Recomputing a block in isolation — resetting the accumulator, or
    keeping only the block just seen — throws away every earlier block's
    contribution and returns a pair no split of the sequence agrees with.

DESIGN DECISION — why do the KV blocks travel an all-gather ring, and why does
the per-hop length count the heads and the head dimension?
    Every rank needs every block, and the ring does that in `split - 1` steps:
    each step every rank forwards one block to its successor, so after `split - 1`
    steps the blocks have visited every rank exactly once. That is `plans.py`'s
    `allgather`, and pricing it with stage 1 charges the real hop. The block a
    rank sends is the key and the value of its positions: `2 * (seq / split) *
    heads * head_dim` elements per batch sample. A length that ignores the heads
    or the head dimension prices one scalar per position and undercounts the
    traffic by the width of the model; a plan that charges nothing has pretended
    the blocks never moved.

DESIGN DECISION — why must the split divide the sequence, and why is the group
the first `split` ranks?
    The ring this stage prices is even: every rank owns the same `seq / split`
    positions, so its block is the same length and the exchange is symmetric. A
    `split` that does not divide `seq` would need a ragged ring with per-rank
    lengths, which is the uneven-exchange exercise of stage 8 and not this one —
    it is refused, naming `seq` and `split`. The group is the ranks that own
    blocks, so a `split` of one is the empty plan of one rank and costs no comms
    at all, exactly as an axis of one does everywhere in the course.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the step charge no compute?
    The step this stage returns is the KV exchange, and the quantity the course
    compares across axes is what crosses the fabric — the ring's hops and the
    bytes on them. The attention arithmetic a rank runs beside that exchange is
    a function of the sequence and the model, not of the ring's schedule, so it
    is added once when the axes are composed in stage 10's report and not
    double-charged here. `compute` is therefore 0 and `step_ticks` reads the
    comms alone, exactly as an axis of one with no collectives costs nothing.

TODO: implement `online_attention` and `context_parallel`.
"""

import model
import plans
import stage_01


def online_attention(blocks):
    """The exact `(numerator, denominator)` pair the whole sequence's attention
    accumulates, from the blocks a rank has seen.

    `blocks` is a non-empty tuple of blocks; a block is a `(q_block, k_block,
    v_block)` triple of equal-length non-empty tuples of ints, the key and value
    of that stretch of the sequence and the queries that attend them. Flattened
    in order the blocks give the whole sequences `q`, `k` and `v`, and the answer
    must be `model.reference_attention(q, k, v)` — the same ints — whatever the
    split is. The accumulation is block by block with a running pivot: the
    weights are `2 ** (score - pivot)` and both `num` and `den` shift by the
    difference when the pivot drops. A malformed block is refused with a
    `model.ModelError` naming the offender.
    """

    """The `StepPlan` of the KV blocks travelling the ring, priced by stage 1.

    The sequence is cut into `split` equal blocks over the first `split` ranks;
    `plans.allgather` walks the key and value blocks around the ring in `split -
    1` steps, one block per rank per step, and the collective's length is the
    elements a rank moves in all, `(split - 1) * block`. A `split` the sequence
    does not divide, a `split` larger than the world, a non-positive `batch`,
    `seq` or `split`, and a `shape` that is not a `ModelShape` are refused with a
    `model.ModelError` naming the offender; a `split` of one is the empty plan.
    """

"""Distributed Training From Scratch — stage 10: The configuration

The nine stages before this one each answer *one* axis: how to cut the gradient
across data-parallel ranks, how to shard the training state, how to split a
block across tensor-parallel ranks, how to stream micro-batches through pipeline
stages, how to route tokens to experts, how to rotate KV blocks around a ring.
This stage answers the question a practitioner actually starts with: **given
this model and this many devices, which split of `(dp, tp, pp, ep, cp)` should
run?**

The answer is not a rule of thumb. `configure(shape, world, *, gpus)` enumerates
every split of the devices across the five axes, composes each split's step out
of the plans the earlier stages built — the dp axis's bucketed gradient
all-reduce (stage 2) or the ZeRO/FSDP gather-scatter ladder (stages 3 and 4), the
tensor block's two all-reduces (stage 5), the pipeline's sends (the schedule
stage 6 defines), the expert dispatch and combine (stage 8) and the KV ring
(stage 9) — prices each one with **stage 1's** `step_ticks`, throws away the ones
that cannot be built and the ones that cannot fit the memory budget, and returns
the `(axes, plan)` of the cheapest survivor. An axis of one contributes nothing
at all: it emits no collective and shards no state, which is why `gpus=1` is
exactly the single-device reference. `report(shape, world, plan)` then reads one
plan back and derives `step_ticks`, `compute`, `comms`, `bytes_per_rank` and
`memory_by_rank` from the plan itself.

DESIGN DECISION — why choose by ticking every candidate instead of by a rule of
thumb?
    "Use tensor parallel for a small model, data parallel for a big one" is
    folklore that is wrong on most fabrics: the same split of the same axes costs
    different ticks on a ring, a tree, a two-level switch and a full mesh,
    because a group's price is the route its own links take. The only honest
    chooser is the argmin of the price over the candidates, computed from the
    plan the rank would actually run. So `configure` enumerates every
    factorization of `gpus` into the five axes (no axis privileged, the rest of
    the space included), builds each split's plan, prices it with stage 1
    (`max(compute, comms)`, never the sum) and keeps the least. A tie goes to the
    lexicographically first tuple, which is a stated rule and not a preference.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the dp axis sized on the *local* shard rather than the
whole model?
    A data-parallel collective reduces the gradient the rank holds, and after the
    other axes have sharded the weights that gradient is the model divided by
    `tp * pp * ep`. Pricing the all-reduce on the whole model would charge the
    step for bytes no rank ever holds, and would make data parallel look
    catastrophically worse than it is in every composed configuration. So the
    axis's buckets (stage 2's rule), its reduce-scatter and its all-gather (stage
    3's and stage 4's rules) all size on `ceil_div(params, tp * pp * ep)` — and
    when nothing else shards the model, the composed plan *is* stage 2's own
    plan, bucket for bucket, byte for byte.

DESIGN DECISION — why does a configuration that cannot fit refuse instead of
being returned?
    A split that does not fit is not a slow configuration, it is one that cannot
    run: the optimizer state is 8 bytes per parameter per rank and does not care
    how elegant the split is. Silently returning it would make the chooser a
    liar, so a split whose ledger exceeds `memory_budget` is refused with a
    `model.ModelError` naming the axis that shards the overflowing kind least,
    the bytes it wants and the budget it has. In the free search the same test
    drops the candidate instead of raising, and when *no* candidate fits the
    refusal names the smallest one, because "nothing fits" must say by how much.

DESIGN DECISION — why must the report recompute instead of read numbers the
configuration already knows?
    This is the defect class the stage exists to catch: a report that declares
    `step_ticks` or `bytes_per_rank` from the configuration's own arithmetic
    agrees with itself and disagrees with the plan the moment anything about the
    plan changes — a bucket boundary, a group, an algorithm. `report` takes only
    the plan and the fabric, and every number it returns is stage 1's own: the
    price of the plan's collectives, the sum of the collectives' ticks, the
    per-rank bytes of its `length`s, and the ledger its `memory` lines already
    are. Two calls return equal reports, and a plan that moves nothing reports
    that nothing moved.

DESIGN DECISION — why does an axis of one cost nothing, and why is that a check
rather than a comment?
    A group of one rank needs no collective (nothing crosses the fabric), no
    shard (the rank already holds everything). Every axis is therefore guarded
    by its own size, and the check asserts it: a plan whose axes hold an axis of
    one must not carry a single collective belonging to that axis. Without the
    guard a `tp=1` would charge the block for an all-reduce over one rank and
    `gpus=1` would stop being the reference the whole course is measured
    against.

"""

#: The five axes, in the order a configuration tuple writes them.
AXIS_ORDER = ("dp", "tp", "pp", "ep", "cp")

#: The default per-device memory budget, in bytes: eight gibibytes.

#: The default gradient bucket, in bytes: stage 2's own threshold.
DEFAULT_BUCKET_BYTES = 25_000_000

#: The ZeRO ladder the dp axis runs on: 0 plain data parallel, 1 ZeRO-1, 2

def configure(shape, world, *, gpus, memory_budget=DEFAULT_MEMORY_BUDGET,

    pipeline parallel's sends (stage 6's schedule), expert parallel's dispatch

    """

files.codecraft/api.py:
"""The tiny API an authored course uses to describe its stages.

A course is a directory containing `course.py`:

    from codecraft.api import stage

    TITLE = "Build a Bloom Filter"
    DESCRIPTION = "A probabilistic set, from hashing to false-positive math."

    def check_1():
        from bloom import BloomFilter
        bf = BloomFilter(bits=64, hashes=2)
        bf.add("x")
        assert "x" in bf
        assert "y" not in bf, "a fresh filter must not report false members"

    STAGES = [
        stage(
            1,
            file="bloom.py",
            title="add and contains",
            tags=["hashing", "data-structure"],
            action="Implement add() to set the k bit positions.",
            predict="can contains() ever be certain an item is absent?",
            hints=["bits = bits[:] to avoid shared state",
                   "use one hash salt per position"],
            check=check_1,
        ),
        ...
    ]

`codecraft run <course>` imports this file, runs each `check`, records the
attempt, and hands the result to the adaptive engine. `hints` are optional —
when omitted, the engine generates them from `action`/`predict`.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional


@dataclass
class Stage:
    id: int
    file: str
    title: str
    check: Callable[[], None]
    tags: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    action: str = ""
    predict: str = ""
    hints: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    solution: Optional[str] = None   # e.g. "solutions/bloom.py: BloomFilter.add"

    def meta(self) -> Dict[str, object]:
        return {
            "file": self.file,
            "title": self.title,
            "tags": list(self.tags),
            "action": self.action,
            "predict": self.predict,
            "hints": list(self.hints),
            "solution": self.solution,
        }


def stage(id: int, file: str, title: str, check: Callable[[], None],
          tags: Optional[List[str]] = None, action: str = "", predict: str = "",
          hints: Optional[List[str]] = None,
          solution: Optional[str] = None) -> Stage:
    """Convenience constructor so course.py stays readable."""
    return Stage(
        id=id, file=file, title=title, check=check, tags=list(tags or []),
        action=action, predict=predict, hints=list(hints or []),
        solution=solution,
    )
